domain: Political Economy / State Formation / Linguistic Engineering
topic_summary: Analysis of Turkey's 1928 alphabet reform (Law 1353), which replaced Arabic script with Latin script within three months via top-down state imposition. The reform achieved rapid literacy gains but severed access to Ottoman literary heritage and created enforcement mechanisms targeting non-compliance. Tests whether a commitment system kernel can be installed with zero prior occupancy of the new reading.

key_entities: Mustafa Kemal Atatürk (state founder; reform architect)
Language Commission / Dil Encümeni (technical implementation body)
Millet Mektepleri / Nation's Schools (mass literacy apparatus)
Latin script (imposed orthography; zero prior Turkish practitioners)
key_tensions: Rapid implementation (3-month mandate) vs gradual transition (5-year commission proposal)
Literacy gains (8% to 20% in 7 years) vs cultural severance (Ottoman heritage inaccessible)
Secular modernization vs Islamic unity (1923 rejection grounds)
State coercion (2-6 month imprisonment) vs voluntary adoption

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: The orthographic substrate through which Turkish language is encoded and transmitted — the shared commitment that written Turkish must use some script system
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: State monopoly on legitimate orthography; Atatürk's personal authority as founder; Language Commission technical legitimacy
commitment_system_recognition.kernel_collapse_reason: Initial analysis identified potential readings (Arabic-script continuity vs Latin-script modernization vs gradual bilingual transition), but these collapse under §1.3-K coherence test. The Arabic-script reading had ZERO institutional defenders after 1928 — no authority structure claiming interpretive legitimacy for Arabic orthography survived the reform. The 'gradual transition' reading was a procedural proposal (5-year timeline), not a competing orthographic commitment. What appeared to be contested readings were actually: (1) an extinct reading with no post-1928 authority structure, (2) a timing dispute within the Latin-script reading, not a separate reading. The kernel was not contested — it was displaced. No pair of readings shares a common substrate while emitting different constraints; the Arabic reading was eliminated, not coexisting. This is state-imposed kernel replacement, not kernel contestation.

omegas.description: Is the kernel/reading framework applicable when one reading is eliminated rather than coexisting? The Arabic-script reading had no post-1928 authority structure — this is displacement, not contestation. Framework may require extension to handle extinct readings vs contested readings.

Would a 5-year gradual transition (Language Commission proposal) have preserved heritage access while achieving literacy gains? Atatürk's claim that 'everyone will read that bit in the old writing' suggests gradual transition would fail — but this is untested assertion, not measured outcome.
omegas.source: Deferred axis secularization_coupling; orthographic_displacement_velocity structural delta

omegas.description: Is the literacy rate increase (8% to 20%, 1927-1935) causally attributable to script change, or to mass education infrastructure (Millet Mektepleri)? Phonemic simplicity claim (3 years to months) is plausible but confounded by simultaneous expansion of state education apparatus.

Is heritage_severance_mechanism a true Mountain (irreversible physical constraint) or a Piton of policy choice? Mass translation programs or mandatory Ottoman Turkish education could restore archive access — severance is contingent on state resource allocation, not physics.

Is disproportionate enforcement against Kurdish populations (deferred axis enforcement_coercion_gradient) a bug or feature? If feature, the reform may be a Snare targeting minority linguistic autonomy, not merely a literacy optimization.
omegas.source: Deferred axis enforcement_coercion_gradient; Dark Matter Probe 3 (Beneficiary Scan)
